content: Coffee ground vomiting refers to a specific appearance of vomit that resembles coffee grounds. This occurs due to the presence of blood that has been exposed to gastric acid for a period of time. Blood contains iron within heme molecules in red blood cells, and when this iron is exposed to gastric acid, it undergoes oxidation. The oxidation process gives the vomitus its characteristic coffee ground appearance. This phenomenon is a classic indicator of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. For instance, a peptic ulcer may bleed into the stomach, leading to the production of coffee ground vomitus. In contrast, the vomiting of bright red blood is referred to as hematemesis. Hematemesis suggests that the upper gastrointestinal bleeding is more acute, more severe, or originates closer to the esophagus or stomach. An example of this would be bleeding caused by a Mallory-Weiss tear in the esophagus. Additionally, oxidized blood from an upper gastrointestinal bleed can be excreted in the stool. This results in the production of tarry, black stools, a condition known as melena.
